active_paradigms.idea: Implement Causal Kalman Filter with Adaptive Process Noise
active_paradigms.description: Implement a one-pass causal Kalman filter using numpy that models the signal as a random walk with measurement noise. The key innovation is adaptive process noise variance estimation based on local signal volatility - when the signal changes rapidly, increase process noise to track faster; when stable, decrease it for smoother output. This directly minimizes lag error (α₂=0.2) and average tracking error (α₃=0.2) while the state prediction naturally smooths noise. The filter uses a simple state-space model: x[n+1] = x[n] + w, y[n] = x[n] + v, where w and v are process and measurement noise. Update equations compute Kalman gain, state estimate, and error covariance at each sample. The adaptive noise estimation uses local differences to estimate signal volatility and scales process noise accordingly.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error and average tracking error by using optimal state estimation; reduce false reversals through smooth state transitions
active_paradigms.cautions: Initialize covariance properly; ensure adaptive noise scaling doesn't cause instability; handle edge cases where signal is too short; the filter naturally introduces some lag which affects alignment in evaluator

active_paradigms.idea: Savitzky-Golay Filter with Optimized Window and Polynomial Order
active_paradigms.description: Use scipy.signal.savgol_filter which fits polynomials locally to smooth while preserving signal derivatives and shape. This directly addresses slope change minimization (α₁=0.3) and false reversal penalty (α₄=0.3) by maintaining the underlying signal trend. The key is selecting optimal window size (odd, 15-31) and polynomial order (3-5) that balance smoothness with responsiveness. Unlike simple moving averages, Savitzky-Golay preserves peak locations and signal curvature, reducing spurious directional reversals. Implement with edge handling (mode='nearest' or 'extend') to handle boundaries. The filter is causal when applied with proper padding, minimizing lag error.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes and false reversals by preserving signal shape and derivatives; maintain tracking accuracy through polynomial fitting
active_paradigms.cautions: Window size must be odd and less than signal length; polynomial order must be less than window size; higher order preserves more detail but may overfit noise; test multiple configurations to find optimal balance

active_paradigms.idea: Frequency-Domain Filtering with Adaptive Threshold Using FFT
active_paradigms.description: Use scipy.fft to transform signal to frequency domain, identify and attenuate high-frequency noise components while preserving low-frequency signal trends. The approach: compute FFT, estimate noise floor from high-frequency components, apply adaptive threshold to suppress noise frequencies, inverse FFT to reconstruct filtered signal. This is fundamentally different from time-domain filtering and can achieve better noise-to-signal separation. For real-time processing, use overlapping windowed FFT with proper phase compensation to minimize lag. The adaptive threshold scales with estimated signal power to preserve genuine high-frequency components while removing noise. This directly targets noise reduction and slope change minimization.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Noise reduction and slope changes by separating signal from noise in frequency domain; preserve signal trends through selective frequency attenuation
active_paradigms.cautions: FFT introduces circular convolution effects; use windowing and overlap to minimize artifacts; phase compensation is critical for minimizing lag; handle edge effects carefully; ensure real-valued output after inverse FFT

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.lfilter with custom one-sided causal filter coefficients
tried_paradigms.description: Design a custom causal filter using lfilter that emphasizes recent samples to minimize lag while still reducing noise. Create exponential decay coefficients that heavily weight recent samples (e.g., decay factor 0.8-0.9) to track signal changes quickly. Unlike symmetric filters, this one-sided approach processes only available data at each point, minimizing the lag penalty. Normalize coefficients to ensure unity gain. This approach directly targets the lag_error metric by reducing the effective delay compared to symmetric window filters. Combine with a light secondary smoothing pass if needed for noise reduction.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: lag_error, avg_error - one-sided filtering minimizes delay while still providing noise reduction
tried_paradigms.cautions: One-sided filters may introduce different types of artifacts. Test different decay factors. Ensure coefficients sum to 1 for unity gain. May need post-processing for very noisy signals.

tried_paradigms.description: Replace the weighted moving average with Savitzky-Golay filter from scipy.signal. This filter fits a polynomial to data within each window, preserving higher-order moments and reducing lag compared to simple averaging. Use polynomial order 2 or 3 with the same window_size to smooth noise while maintaining signal dynamics and reducing false reversals. The polynomial fit naturally predicts the current point rather than averaging past values, which significantly reduces L_recent and L_avg lag errors. Set polyorder=2 for a balance between smoothing and responsiveness.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (L_recent, L_avg) and slope changes (S) - the Savitzky-Golay filter reduces lag by fitting polynomials rather than averaging, and preserves trend changes better than moving averages
tried_paradigms.cautions: Window size must be odd and greater than polyorder. If window_size=20, use window_size=19 or 21. Handle edge cases where signal length is less than window size. The filter may overshoot at sharp transitions - consider clamping or blending with original signal at detected edges.

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement Kalman filter with adaptive noise estimation
tried_paradigms.description: Build a 2-state Kalman filter (position and velocity) that recursively estimates the true signal state. Initialize state covariance Q (process noise) and R (measurement noise) based on observed signal statistics. At each step, predict the next state using the velocity model, then update with the noisy measurement. The Kalman gain automatically balances trust between prediction and measurement, minimizing lag while filtering noise. This approach is optimal for Gaussian noise and handles non-stationary signals by continuously adapting. Compute R from initial signal variance and set Q to allow reasonable velocity changes.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (L_recent, L_avg) and false reversals (R) - Kalman filter provides optimal estimation with minimal lag, and the state model prevents spurious direction changes caused by noise
tried_paradigms.cautions: Must handle the first window_size samples carefully - either use initial estimates or run filter from start. The state transition matrix assumes constant velocity which may not hold for all signals. Tune Q/R ratio: higher Q means faster tracking but more noise, lower Q means smoother but more lag.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.medfilt with adaptive window and post-smoothing
tried_paradigms.description: Apply median filtering (scipy.signal.medfilt) first to remove outliers and sharp noise spikes without introducing lag, then apply a light exponential smoothing pass. Median filtering preserves edges and step changes better than mean-based filters, reducing false reversals. Use an odd kernel size slightly smaller than window_size (e.g., 15 or 17) to maintain responsiveness. Follow with a very light exponential moving average (alpha=0.3) to smooth remaining high-frequency noise. This two-stage approach combines robustness with smoothness.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: False reversals (R) and slope changes (S) - median filter is robust to outliers and preserves genuine trend changes, while the light post-smoothing reduces spurious small reversals
tried_paradigms.cautions: Median filter requires odd kernel size. The kernel size affects latency - keep it close to but smaller than window_size. Median filtering alone may leave some high-frequency noise, hence the need for light post-smoothing. Ensure the exponential smoothing doesn't reintroduce significant lag.

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement Causal Kalman Filter with numpy
tried_paradigms.description: Implement a 1D Kalman filter using numpy that tracks both signal value and velocity. The Kalman filter is specifically designed for real-time tracking with minimal lag and naturally adapts to signal dynamics. State vector is [position, velocity], with prediction step using velocity and update step incorporating new measurements. Process noise and measurement noise can be tuned based on local signal characteristics. This approach fundamentally differs from failed filter attempts because it uses state-space modeling rather than convolution-based filtering. The filter produces causal output with minimal delay, directly improving lag error metrics.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (L_recent) and tracking accuracy (correlation with clean signal) while maintaining low slope changes
tried_paradigms.cautions: Initialize state and covariance matrices properly. Tune process noise (Q) and measurement noise (R) based on signal characteristics. Ensure numerical stability for long sequences.

tried_paradigms.description: Implement rule-based trend detection with hysteresis thresholds to prevent false reversals. Calculate signal trend direction, then only allow trend changes when the signal crosses a hysteresis threshold (e.g., must exceed current value by margin M in opposite direction). This directly targets the false reversal penalty (R) which has high weight (0.3). Combine with light smoothing to reduce noise while preserving genuine trend changes. The hysteresis margin can be adaptive based on local noise level. This approach is rule-based rather than filter-based, making it fundamentally different from failed filter attempts.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: False reversal penalty (R) and slope changes (S) - both have 0.3 weight in composite score
tried_paradigms.cautions: Hysteresis threshold must be tuned - too large causes lag, too small allows false reversals. Consider adaptive threshold based on local signal variance.

tried_paradigms.idea: Multi-scale Median Combination with Local Variance Adaptation
tried_paradigms.description: Apply median filtering at multiple kernel sizes (e.g., 3, 7, 15) and combine results with weights based on local signal variance. Calculate local variance in sliding window, use smaller kernels for high-variance regions (preserves edges) and larger kernels for low-variance regions (better smoothing). This multi-scale approach better handles non-stationary signals than single-scale median filtering. The combination can be weighted average or adaptive selection based on which scale best preserves signal characteristics. This differs from failed attempts by using multi-scale analysis rather than single filter.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Balance between slope changes (S) and tracking accuracy (correlation) across different signal regimes
tried_paradigms.cautions: Ensure output length matches expected (len(x) - window_size + 1). Handle edge cases at signal boundaries. Keep computational cost reasonable for multiple scales.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.cwt for wavelet-based denoising with soft thresholding
tried_paradigms.description: Apply Continuous Wavelet Transform (cwt) using Morlet wavelet to decompose the noisy signal into time-frequency components. Apply soft thresholding to wavelet coefficients to remove noise while preserving sharp transitions and trend changes. Reconstruct the signal from thresholded coefficients using inverse transform. This approach is fundamentally different from polynomial smoothing or median filtering as it operates in the time-frequency domain, making it ideal for non-stationary signals with varying frequency content. The wavelet-based approach naturally handles both high-frequency noise and low-frequency trends without introducing significant phase delay.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S) and False reversals (R) - wavelet thresholding preserves genuine trend changes while removing noise-induced reversals
tried_paradigms.cautions: Choose appropriate wavelet scales to match signal characteristics; use soft thresholding with universal threshold (sigma*sqrt(2*log(n))) to avoid over-smoothing; ensure causal reconstruction to minimize lag error

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement adaptive Kalman filter with state-space model [position, velocity]
tried_paradigms.description: Build a discrete-time Kalman filter with state vector containing signal value and its derivative (velocity). Model the signal dynamics as a random walk with adaptive process noise based on local signal volatility. Implement adaptive measurement noise estimation using innovation sequence statistics. The Kalman filter provides optimal minimum-variance estimation for linear Gaussian systems with explicit modeling of signal dynamics. Use alpha-beta-gamma filter variant for computational efficiency, which is equivalent to a simplified Kalman filter for constant acceleration models. This approach minimizes lag error while tracking genuine trends.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (L_recent) and Average tracking error (L_avg) - Kalman filter provides optimal causal estimation with minimal delay
tried_paradigms.cautions: Initialize covariance matrices appropriately; tune process noise (Q) and measurement noise (R) adaptively; ensure numerical stability with cholesky decomposition; handle edge cases at signal boundaries

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.sosfilt with adaptive Butterworth filter design
tried_paradigms.description: Design a causal low-pass Butterworth filter using scipy.signal.butter in second-order sections (SOS) format for numerical stability. Adapt the cutoff frequency based on local signal characteristics (e.g., dominant frequency or volatility). Apply the filter using scipy.signal.sosfilt which is more stable than direct lfilter for higher-order filters. The SOS format prevents numerical issues that can occur with direct IIR filter implementation. Use a causal (forward-only) filter to maintain real-time processing capability while minimizing phase delay. This differs from the failed lfilter approach by using the more numerically stable sosfilt implementation.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Smoothness (S) and Noise reduction - Butterworth filter provides smooth frequency response with good noise attenuation
tried_paradigms.cautions: Use sosfilt instead of lfilter for stability; keep filter order low (2-4) to minimize group delay; adapt cutoff frequency to signal bandwidth; ensure filter coefficients are recomputed for each segment if signal is non-stationary
